title: Judah's Land and Its Towns
overview: This chapter maps out the land given to the tribe of Judah, tells how Caleb and his family took their share, and lists the towns in Judah's territory.

parts.label: Judah's borders (vv. 1-12)
parts.note: Judah's southern edge matches the southern edge of the whole land, facing Edom, with the Dead Sea on the east and the Mediterranean on the west. The northern line passes landmarks like the Valley of Achor, remembered from Achan's story in chapter 7, and runs along the southern slope of Jerusalem.

parts.label: Caleb takes Hebron and Debir (vv. 13-17)
parts.note: Caleb receives the hill town of Hebron, as promised to him in chapter 14, and drives out three Anakite leaders named Sheshai, Ahiman and Talmai, from a people remembered as unusually tall and strong. He then offers his daughter Aksah in marriage to whoever captures nearby Debir, a way of rewarding bravery in that culture, and his relative Othniel wins her.

parts.label: Aksah asks for springs (vv. 18-19)
parts.note: Aksah's land was in the Negev, the dry south, where a field without water was of little use. She asks her father directly for springs, and he gives her the upper and lower springs.

parts.label: Towns of the south and lowlands (vv. 20-47)
parts.note: The town list is grouped by region: first the dry Negev near Edom, then the low rolling foothills to the west. It also names the coastal cities of Ekron, Ashdod and Gaza, though these were Philistine strongholds that Judah rarely if ever controlled.

parts.label: Hill country and wilderness (vv. 48-62)
parts.note: These are the towns of Judah's central highlands, including Hebron and Debir again, plus a few settlements in the harsh desert by the Dead Sea, such as En Gedi with its spring. The list probably reflects how the region was organized into districts, though scholars debate when it was drawn up.

parts.label: Jerusalem not taken (v. 63)
parts.note: The chapter ends by admitting that Judah could not drive the Jebusites out of Jerusalem. The city stayed in their hands until King David captured it generations later, so the land on paper and the land actually held were not the same.

think: Aksah already had land but asked for water to make it livable. What turns a place you have into a place you can actually live well?
